newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy futures exchange seeks way to pump up volume.
newsitem.headline: Italy futures exchange seeks way to pump up volume.

text.p: Italy's languishing financial futures market wants to breathe life into its exchange by tightening requirements for market makers, launching new contracts and linking with other markets.
A task force set up by the Italian futures market, or MIF, is looking at ways to revamp the exchange and is expected to start bringing in changes by the end of September.
The main challenge is MIF's scarce liquidity. Trading has dwindled as many Italian dealers have gravitated towards London's International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE).
MIF was launched in November 1992, just over a year after LIFFE starting trading futures contracts on Italy's benchmark BTP treasury securities.
"The MIF is more transparent and less costly than LIFFE," said a member of the MIF task force, based at the Italian banking association's headquarters.

"The problem is one of scarce autonomy. The MIF market is used for arbitrage operations against LIFFE, with the result that 50 percent of operations by Italians are conducted on the London market," he added.
A key change being considered is tightening requirements for the exchange's 27 market makers who are now only required to show a loosely-defined "significant presence" on the market.
Analysts said the loose definition produces uncommitted market makers, which results in wide spreads and scant trade.
Stricter guidelines would likely ask market makers to quote narrower spreads and guarantee minimum daily volume to continue participating in the market.

"Anyone who really wants to be a market maker has to commit to quoting a limited spread and to trading a given minimum daily volume. In return, the MIF could grant certain exclusive functions to market makers," said Antonio Lengua of Deutsche Bank, who is a member of the task force.
The MIF is also considering ways to increase the number of market makers by either opening the market to dealers operating abroad or letting in all internal dealers.
Other proposals include lower commissions and other incentives for users and new contracts.
Because the MIF's 10-year BTP is the only actively traded contract, traders have difficulty switching from one derivative to another. Trade in the MIF's five-year contract is thin.

"By the end of the month, a new product, perhaps a BOT (Treasury bill) futures contract, could be added to the BTP futures that are already available. Operators want a contract on a short-term security, which the MIF does not currently offer," said a member in one of MIF's working groups.
Other contract ideas include futures pegged to BTP/Bund spreads, interbank deposits and foreign currency.
Another proposal would link the MIF market to the more successful MTS market, which displays market makers' Italian government debt issue prices.

The MIF task force is also working on an agreement, if not a merger, with IDEM, the share derivatives market, and collaborative deals with foreign markets. Deals with Germany's DTB and France's Matif are under study.
"If you want to attract new people, it is indispensable that we offer a single derivatives market," said a member of the management committee.
